h1: The 6 Best Loppers for Thick Branches of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Loppers for Thick Branches: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 6 loppers for thick branches scored on cut capacity, bypass or anvil blades, leverage design, handle length and build quality.
summary: The Corona X Series Pro bypass lopper tops the list with a 2-1/4 inch cut capacity, the biggest here, in a pro-grade build. Fiskars' 32 inch PowerGear2 is the best easy-to-use choice, with leverage that does the work for you. Hickok's 36 inch aluminum loppers add reach, and the AIRAJ extendable anvil model is the budget pick for dead wood. Skip the 28 inch Fiskars for anything beyond 1.5 inches.
intro: The number that matters on a lopper is cut capacity, and the number that misleads is length. A longer handle gives more leverage, but it does not make a 1.5 inch blade cut a 2 inch limb. Many buyers pick the longest tool in the shed aisle and still end up twisting and tearing at a branch the jaws were never rated for.

We reviewed six loppers from their specs, comparing stated cut capacity, blade style, leverage mechanism, handle length and materials. Capacity runs from 1.5 inches to 2-1/4 inches. Bypass blades glide past each other like scissors and suit green wood, while anvil blades crush against a flat surface and suit dead branches. We ranked with that split in mind.

products.name: Corona Tools X Series Pro Bypass Lopper
products.verdict: The largest stated cut capacity here at 2-1/4 inches, with a pro-grade bypass blade.
products.description:
The Corona X Series Pro is a pro-grade bypass lopper with a 2-1/4 inch cut capacity, the biggest in this group, and a heavy-duty branch cutter build.

That extra quarter inch over the 2 inch rivals is real: it is the difference between one clean cut and a second pass on a live limb. It beats the Fiskars 32 inch PowerGear2 on capacity, though the Fiskars is easier on the arms thanks to its leverage system.

Buy it for regular pruning of thick, living branches on fruit trees and shrubs. The caveat is that the listing gives no handle length or weight, so ask before you assume it matches the 32 inch reach of the Fiskars.
pros: Clean bypass cuts on live wood
products.idealFor: Regular pruning of thick living branches.
products.skipIf: You mainly cut dead wood, where an anvil lopper works fine.

products.name: Fiskars 32 in PowerGear2 Bypass Lopper
products.verdict: A 32 inch bypass lopper with PowerGear2 leverage and a 2 inch capacity.
products.description:
The Fiskars is 32 inches long with a bypass blade, a 2 inch cut capacity, PowerGear2 leverage and a low-friction coating.

PowerGear2 is a gear-driven pivot that multiplies force through the stroke, so thick wood needs less squeezing than on a plain pivot. It ranks just below the Corona because capacity is 1/4 inch smaller, but it is the one I would hand to a first-time pruner.

It suits homeowners who cut a few thick branches a season. The caveat is that more moving parts means more to clean, and the price is higher than the 28 inch Fiskars.
products.idealFor: Homeowners who want easier cuts on thick branches.
products.skipIf: You need more than a 2 inch capacity.

products.name: Hickok 36 in Heavy Duty Loppers
products.verdict: Aircraft-grade aluminum handles and a forged, heat-treated steel blade at 36 inches.
products.description:
The Hickok is 36 inches long with aircraft-grade aluminum handles and a forged, heat-treated steel blade.

The 36 inches is the longest in the set, and long handles are the cheapest source of leverage, while aluminum keeps the weight down. It ranks below the Fiskars because the listing gives no cut capacity, so you cannot confirm it handles 2 inch limbs.

It fits people who prune high branches without a ladder. The caveat is the missing capacity figure, plus the price, the highest here.
products.idealFor: Reaching high branches from the ground.
products.skipIf: You need a documented cut capacity.

products.name: TABOR TOOLS GG12A Anvil Compound Lopper
products.verdict: 30 inch handles, an anvil blade and compound action for dead wood.
products.description:
The TABOR GG12A has 30 inch handles, an anvil blade, compound action, rubberized grips and a 2 inch cut capacity.

Anvil blades crush wood against a flat surface, which suits dry, dead branches better than green ones. Compound action multiplies force, so a 2 inch dead branch cuts more easily than it would on a simple pivot. It ranks fourth because anvil cuts are rougher on living wood than the bypass cuts above.

Choose it for clearing dead limbs. The caveat is that crushed cuts on live trees can slow healing.

products.name: AIRAJ 27-37 in Extendable Anvil Loppers
products.verdict: Handles extend from 27 to 37 inches, with SK5 steel and four pivot points.
products.description:
The AIRAJ extends from 27 to 37 inches, uses an anvil blade with compound action, has four pivot points and a 2 inch capacity. The blade is SK5 steel with a Teflon coating.

Extendable handles let one tool serve tight shrubs and high limbs, which none of the fixed-length models here can do. It ranks below the TABOR because extension joints add a place to flex under load.

It works for mixed jobs on a budget. The caveat is that anvil cuts crush living wood, and the extension lock needs checking.
products.idealFor: Mixed pruning jobs from shrubs to high limbs.
products.skipIf: You want a one-piece, rigid handle.

products.name: Fiskars 28 in Garden Bypass Lopper
products.verdict: The cheapest bypass lopper here, but capped at 1.5 inches.
products.description:
The Fiskars 28 in is a bypass lopper with a 1.5 inch cut capacity, a low-friction coating and a non-slip grip.

It is the shortest and least capable lopper here, which is why it ranks last for thick branches. Against the 32 inch Fiskars it loses half an inch of capacity and four inches of reach.

It is an honest tool for shrubs and saplings. The caveat is plain: a 1.5 inch limit means it is the wrong tool for the thick branches this ranking targets.
products.idealFor: Light pruning of shrubs and saplings.

methodology.title: Cut capacity
methodology.description: Stated maximum branch diameter is the first filter for a ranking about thick branches.

methodology.title: Blade style
methodology.description: Bypass suits live wood and anvil suits dead wood, so we reward the right match for the job.

methodology.title: Leverage
methodology.description: Gear, compound action and handle length determine how much effort a thick cut takes.

methodology.title: Materials
methodology.description: Forged steel, aluminum handles and blade coatings affect weight and durability.

methodology.title: Listing clarity
methodology.description: Loppers that publish capacity and length earn higher marks than those that do not.

whatMatters.detail: Cut capacity is the maximum branch diameter the jaws are designed to sever in one stroke. Pushing past it twists the blades and dulls the edge. Read the stated figure, such as 2 inches or 2-1/4 inches, and choose a lopper rated above your thickest branch, not equal to it, so you are not working at the limit.

A bypass blade slides past a hook like scissors and leaves a clean cut on live wood, which heals faster. An anvil blade closes onto a flat edge and crushes, which is quicker on dry, dead limbs. Match the blade to the wood you cut most, and check the listing's blade-type line.

Force at the blades depends on handle length and the pivot design. Compound action and gear systems such as PowerGear2 multiply force without making the tool longer. If you cut thick wood often, prefer a mechanism over raw length, since a gear system reduces effort at every stroke.

Long loppers get heavy, and fatigue makes cuts sloppy. Aluminum handles, as on the Hickok, cut weight without losing strength, while steel is heavier but cheaper. Check the handle material and length on the listing, and add weight if the maker omits it.

A low-friction or Teflon coating cuts the drag of sap and prevents rust. Forged, heat-treated steel holds an edge longer than stamped metal. Look for words like forged, heat-treated, SK5 or coating on the listing, and wipe sap off the blade after every session.

faq.q: Can any of these loppers cut a 3 inch branch?
faq.a: No. The largest stated capacity is the Corona's 2-1/4 inches. Anything thicker needs a pruning saw, because forcing a lopper past its rating damages the blades and the pivot.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake with loppers?
faq.a: Using an anvil lopper like the TABOR on living branches. It crushes the wood, which heals slowly. Use a bypass model such as the Fiskars 32 inch for green limbs.

faq.q: Is PowerGear2 worth it over the Corona?
faq.a: Only for ease. The Fiskars 32 inch PowerGear2 reduces effort, but the Corona offers 1/4 inch more capacity. If your branches stay near 2 inches, the Fiskars is gentler on arms.

faq.q: How do I set up the extendable AIRAJ?
faq.a: Extend the handles to the length you need, lock the joint fully and test with a light cut before a thick one. Check the lock periodically, since extension joints can loosen with use.

faq.q: How do I maintain a lopper?
faq.a: Wipe sap from the blade after use, dry it and add light oil to the pivots. Coated blades such as the Fiskars low-friction or AIRAJ Teflon finish clean easily, but still rust if stored wet.

faq.q: Are the 36 inch Hickok loppers good for thick limbs?
faq.a: They offer excellent leverage, but the listing states no cut capacity. Ask the seller for the figure first, because length alone does not guarantee the jaws will handle a 2 inch limb.

finalTake: The Corona X Series Pro bypass lopper is the right buy for thick, living branches because its 2-1/4 inch capacity is the largest here. The Fiskars 32 inch PowerGear2 is the easier, friendlier pick, and the TABOR is the anvil choice for dead wood. Skip the 28 inch Fiskars for anything thick.
